metadata.title: Small Block and Big Block Engines Explained | Tech Talk
metadata.description:
Do you know the difference between a small and big block engine? Watch the video to find out what it is, why it matters, and how to know which one you need!

#SmallBlock #BigBlock #CarEngine #CarExpert

Get everything you need for your Mustang here:
https://www.cjponyparts.com/mustang-p...

Subscribe for more Tech Talks!
http://www.youtube.com/subscription_c...

Read the article for more info:
https://www.cjponyparts.com/resources...

Music Provided By:
https://elements.envato.com/curated

captions.text: On today's tech talk we're going to discuss engine displacement and the difference between a small block and big block engine. So a while back we did a poll talking about what kind of engine you guys wanted us to see in project Betty. We talked about doing a small block, a big block mod motor, a coyote, we talked about the Godzilla motor possibly even an EcoBoost. A couple different options came up and a lot of people actually asked what is the difference between a small block and a big block as far as a build like that would go. I start thinking about it, it's like you know what, what's the difference. Well the big block's bigger obviously; this is a big block Ford, this would be a small block Ford. You can see you know the block is bigger the crank is massively bigger. You know the heads will be larger the valves will be bigger, but what makes it a big block? What separates the big block from the small block is it cubic inches well it isn't. That's where displacement comes into play. You can have a 396 cubic inch big block and you can have a 400 cubic inch small block, and there's several other setups as well. You know Fords if you get into the stroke or Windsors you get a 408, even bigger motors that are all still considered small blocks, or like I said you have a 390 a 396 a bunch of smaller big blocks. So what's the difference well let's take a look at both these blocks and go to some details. So what's the difference like we said the big block is physically bigger we'd say you know bigger block bigger heads bigger valves bigger crank end of video. Let's talk about displacement now the two engines we have in front of us here we're going to call this a 429 which actually is this one's going to be our 302. Now if you actually know what you're looking at you might notice this is a dart block this is obviously a little bit bigger but it's what our machine shop handy so again for video purposes this will be our big block 429 and this will be our small block 302. So let's talk about displacement displacement is a measurement it can be cubic inches, Now your pistons connect to your rods and connect your crank and they're going to move at different speeds but that volume never changes. So how do you figure out displacement? Well displacement there's going to be a formula for it; there's a couple different ones you can use. We're going to use 0.7854 you're going to times that by the bore. Now the bore is going to be the width of the cylinder here so basically however wide this is that's going to be your bore. So what you can do is do 0.7854 times the bore squared and we're going to times it by the stroke. The stroke is how far the piston moves in and out of the cylinder, so again that comes down to the crankshaft that's where the term stroker comes from--we'll get to that later--but basically the All right so let's talk about a Stroker motor. The most common one in the Ford family is going to be the 347, everyone's heard of that, they call it a stroke. Why is it a stroker well you're going to change some things in the block to create the stroker. Like I said with a regular 302 your bore is going to be four inches and the stroke inside here is going to be three inches. Now how do you get a stroker motor, well you increase the stroke in this case you increase the bore as well. Now with a small block basically you're limited on how much you can open these up. Your factory bore spacing onto 302 is 4.38 inches so basically the center of this hole the center of this hole is going to be 4.38, so when you're actually going to bore these out for a bored stroker motor you can see you only have so much material to go with. So the 347 is going to take this and take it from a four inch bore to a four point zero three so when someone says 30 over that's actually what they're talking about. Thirty thousandths larger again require a custom piston but then you're also going to change the stroke from three inches to three point four. So you're changing the crank it's basically going to change the stroke and that's how you get the additional cubic inches. Now here we have our big block Ford, now again like I said before obviously physically larger. Now big blocks were originally designed for larger sedans and for trucks because they wanted a bigger engine, more cubic inches, more physical engine size to move the heavy vehicles. Obviously hot rodders got hold of big blocks, started sticking them in small lightweight cars the manufacturers followed and basically that's where the muscle cars came from. Most of the most desirable muscle cars had big block engines because in a lightweight car they made them nice and fast. Now here this is a 429 big block Ford, and again you can see the bore spacing huge huge difference there's a lot more material in here but it's also larger to begin with. Now this is going to be a 4.36 inch four so much larger than our small block and a 3.59 stroke so again much larger. Now combine that with the eight cylinder engine and do the math and it comes out to 428.79 somewhere in the neighborhood which basically is a 429 but also you can see by the four spacing there's a lot more room in this big block now up close you can see a huge difference in the bore spacing like i said our small block you're talking about 4.38 inches the big block is 4.9 so there's a lot more meat there a lot more material that could be ground away to put a much larger piston in you could actually go much much larger with the bores go with a stroke or crank and make a lot more cubic inches than you can do with a typical small block so when it comes down to your conventional factory built blocks you know the limit on a small block is going to be in the low 400 cubic inches where big blocks you can go well over 500 cubes now after market blocks there's a lot of different options there but again talk with more of the conventional factory reduced blocks most motors over 400 are going to be your big block where a lot of your small blocks will be under 400. so for our build we decided to go with a small block what we're building is going to be a 331 so like the 347 we discussed the 331 is going to have a 30 overboard so that board's going to go four inches to 4.030 the stroke will be 3.25 inches instead of 3.4 so a little bit less stroke than 347 but still a stroker motor now 331 versus 347 we won't get into that there's tons of articles out there you can read up on it we talked to our engine builder about the car what we're gonna do and that's what he suggested and we're gonna go with that setup now which one's right for your car depends what you're gonna do now the benefits your big block engine are obviously going to be larger cubic inches you're talking larger valves a ton of torque the benefit of the small block and the reason we went with it a lot of it has to do with weight now your 302 based engine it's going to be a lot smaller and a lot lighter than the big block and for car that we're trying to build for handling purposes and to be a really good street car the small block fit what we were looking to do now again the big block unlimited cubic inches tons of torque but it's a heavy rotating assembly so you're not going to get a ton of rpm out of it unless you go to really really exotic components where again your small block you get a lot more rpm out of it at a lot more reasonable cost you're going to give up some torque but again then we're getting the power adders which can be a whole different video but again they say there's no replacement for displacement a lot of the turbo and supercharger companies might actually argue that but either way whether you're looking to build a small block or a big block both can be the right solution for your mustang you
